pending_articles.title: Selective Nerve Block of A- or C-Afferents Confirms Dual Role in Touch Pleasantness but Not Touch-Pain Modulation
pending_articles.content: Gentle and deep pressure are distinct types of touch that often elicit pleasant sensations and modulate pain. Although touch pleasantness has traditionally been attributed to unmyelinated C-tactile afferents, growing evidence suggests an important contribution of myelinated A-fibers. However, the relative role of A- and C-fibers in touch-evoked pleasantness and pain modulation remains unclear. To test the role of A- and C-fibers in touch pleasantness, healthy adults underwent selective peripheral nerve block of the superficial radial nerve to preferentially impair either A- or C-fiber function. Touch pleasantness of brushing (Study 1; N = 24) or deep pressure (Study 2; N = 24) and touch-induced modulation of heat pain were assessed before and after the nerve block. Both nerve blocks significantly reduced the perceived pleasantness of both gentle brushing and deep pressure, supporting a substantial contribution of myelinated A-fibers and well as unmyelinated C-fibers (presumably C-tactile fibers) to affective touch. In addition, block of A-fibers did not diminish touch-induced modulation of experimental heat pain, suggesting a particular pain-inhibiting role for C-tactile fibers. These findings supply causal evidence in healthy adults that myelinated A-fibers are highly involved in touch pleasantness-alongside C-tactile fibers-but are not involved in touch-induced pain relief.
pending_articles.author: Albinni, B., Crankshaw, L. N., Jones, E., Alasha, V., Zimmerman, M., Schuster, N., Said, E., Strigo, I., Case, L. K.

pending_articles.title: Short-term cortical stimulation combined with targeted rehabilitation and Chondroitinase ABC improves upper limb function following a cervical contusion injury
pending_articles.content: Spinal cord injuries (SCI) at the cervical level can lead to permanent upper limb and hand motor impairments, thus restoring upper limb function is amongst the highest priorities for SCI patients and can have extensive effects on improving quality of life and patient independence. We previously showed that long-term cortical stimulation of the motor cortex (10 weeks) when applied in conjunction with a daily upper limb targeted rehabilitation regiment and a neuroplasticity enhancing therapy such as lentiviral Chondroitinase ABC (ChABC) can lead to an increase of muscle activity which was translated to restored skilled function after a clinically relevant contusion injury. Here, we investigate the effects of a short term cortical stimulation protocol as part of the same neurorehabilitation paradigm to asses its efficecy. Adult rats were implanted unilaterally with stimulating electrodes (contralaterally to the dominant forepaw as determined by skilled reaching) on the surface of the motor cortex and received a bilateral cervical (C5/C6) contusion injury to produce severe and long lasting forelimb motor deficits. Contused animals received acute intraspinal injections of the neuroplasticity promoting agent ChABC and 12 consecutives days of epidural electrical stimulation of the motor cortex along with daily targeted upper limb behavioural rehabilitation (Whishaw Window and Montoya staircase, 15 minutes for 5 days/week for 7 weeks) starting at 7 days post injury. Our results revealed marked improvements in the tasks specific for assessing upper limb dexterity. These were also corroborated by electrophysiological and anatomical evidence. Thus, we provide robust evidence that short term cortical epidural stimulation as part of a combinational neurorehabilitation paradigm can restore upper limb function after a cervical contusion.
pending_articles.author: sinopoulou, e., Burnside, E. R., Bartus, K., Bradbury, E. J.

pending_articles.title: The Cost to Scroll: Short-form Video Use and Episodic Memory
pending_articles.content: Short-form video platforms expose users to rapid streams of novel content; these features are posited to place heavy demands on cognitive processes. In a preregistered online study, we used device-reported screen time to examine whether short-form video use is associated with sustained attention and episodic memory in participants aged 18-24 yrs (N = 502). During a sustained attention task, participants made indoor/outdoor decisions on scene stimuli, with 90% frequent trials and 10% infrequent trials; the subsequent surprise recognition test assessed memory for these items. Among participants with device-reported TikTok or Instagram use (N = 398), short-form video use was not associated with attention performance. By contrast, greater short-form video use was associated with poorer episodic memory; this relationship was driven by poorer recognition of infrequent-category items. These findings connect heavier short-form video consumption with poorer episodic memory in young adults, showing how daily digital habits co-vary with memory function.
pending_articles.author: Chen, K. K., Miller, D. S., Nguyen, K. K., Wagner, A. D., Tran, T. T.

pending_articles.title: Critical scaling of cortical ensembles without cooperative amplification
pending_articles.content: Cortical neurons are sparsely and weakly connected, motivating the long-standing idea that they must act collectively, as cell assemblies, to exert substantial influence on surrounding networks. Yet a few spikes in a single pyramidal neuron can recruit thousands of cortical neurons according to a power law with exponent ~0.285, consistent with a two-dimensional system near a critical percolation transition. Here we holographically stimulated ensembles of 1 to 16 layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons in visual cortex of awake mice while imaging hundreds of neighbouring neurons. Across two orders of magnitude in evoked spike count, network responses followed the same scaling law observed for single-neuron perturbations, with no detectable threshold at which co-activation produced additional amplification. Recruitment was sublinear, suppression increased with ensemble size, and ongoing scale-free avalanche dynamics remained stationary. Nevertheless, ensemble identity became increasingly decodable from surrounding activity. Thus, coordinated firing increases representational specificity without escaping the critical dynamics governing propagation: cortical ensembles convey identity without gaining disproportionate causal impact.
pending_articles.author: Ribeiro, T. L., Siddiqui, R., Gifford, B., Pajevic, S., Plenz, D.

pending_articles.title: Real-time posterior probabilistic TMS motor mapping with robust individualized stopping criteria
pending_articles.content: Background. Electric-field-informed regression provides high-resolution transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) motor maps, but conventional nonlinear fitting is too slow to update the map during acquisition, so sessions rely on predefined stimulation budgets, despite substantial inter-individual variability in the data required for stable localization. Objective. To develop a real-time analysis updating a posterior probability map between pulses and compare its hotspots with finger-tapping functional MRI (fMRI). Methods. We analyzed two independent cohorts (12 and 13 participants, one newly collected), analyzing each hand muscle independently. We replaced the conventional per-element sigmoid fit with Spearman's rank correlation coefficient and transformed the resulting score map into a posterior probability map using marginal-likelihood evidence. Acquisition stopped once posterior mass within 5 mm of the hotspot passed a preset confidence level. Results. The Spearman and linear scores updated the region of interest within milliseconds, versus tens of seconds for sigmoid fitting. Spearman more closely matched the full-data sigmoid hotspot in recorded sessions and converged faster and more precisely to the true source in virtual subjects. Across both fast scores, at a confidence level of 0.85, the stopping criterion was met after a median of 74-159 pulses, with 26-454 across individual problems. FDI hotspots lay 8.3 {+/-} 4.3 mm from the fMRI center of gravity, in the precentral hand region. Conclusions. Rank correlation reduces computation time without loss of accuracy relative to sigmoid fitting. The resulting posterior probability map provides a session-specific stopping criterion in place of a fixed pulse budget.
pending_articles.author: Qiu, R., Feng, Z.-J., Numssen, O., Zang, Y.-F., Wilhelmy, F., Güresir, E., Knösche, T. R., Weise, K.

pending_articles.title: AMPK-dependent brain-wide norepinephrine release promotes recovery from metabolic coma in mice
pending_articles.content: Coma is a pathological brain state characterized by loss of consciousness. How the brain recovers from coma remains largely unknown. Using mouse models of metabolic coma, we identified an endogenous neuromodulatory pathway that actively promotes coma recovery. In mice subjected to hypoglycemic coma, hypoglycemia triggered AMPK-dependent excitation of nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) neurons, which activated locus coeruleus (LC) norepinephrine neurons through a glutamatergic NTS-LC circuit. LC activation drives widespread norepinephrine release across cortical and subcortical regions, thereby promoting post-coma arousal. Notably, coma-associated brain-wide norepinephrine release was unconventional in both scale and duration, with a magnitude approximately 10-fold higher than physiological norepinephrine release during sleep-wake cycles. This neuromodulatory process also operated during hypercapnic coma. Vagus nerve stimulation accelerated coma recovery by engaging this endogenous anti-coma mechanism. Our findings uncover an AMPK-dependent brainstem circuit that actively restores arousal from metabolic coma, revealing a neural defense strategy against profound metabolic stress.
pending_articles.author: Wu, M., Zhang, L., Li, Y., Chen, G., Li, D., Zhao, M., Gu, H., Song, H., Cao, Y., Yang, Z., Liu, Z., Zhang, F., Li, T.-Z., Miao, H.-H., Cao, P.

pending_articles.title: Computational Evaluation of tDCS Montage Separability and Dose Coverage for Practice-Specific Mindfulness Experiments
pending_articles.content: A practice-specific stimulation experiment requires candidate montages that differ in regional electric-field exposure without sacrificing interpretable target dose. We evaluated this requirement for transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) montages intended to test focused-attention and open-monitoring mindfulness practices. Four focused-attention candidates and six open-monitoring candidates formed 24 pairs, evaluated with SimNIBS 4.6 in 20 existing anatomical head models at a linearly scaled current of 2 mA. Outcomes were regional 99th-percentile field magnitude, a normalized double-dissociation index (DDI), suprathreshold overlap, and individual dose coverage. Eighteen pairs passed four recorded progression criteria, but only five also met a post hoc requirement that both intended regional contrasts be positive in at least 80% of heads. A positive DDI alone concealed a reversed salience-region contrast in one conventional comparison. The nominated F3-centered 4-by-1 ring paired with F8-Fp2 sponges (FA-05 x OM-02) produced both directional preferences in 20/20 heads, with median DDI 1.561 and median suprathreshold Dice 0.000. The conventional F3-Fp2 and FT8-FCz sponge pair (FA-02 x OM-07) produced both preferences in 19/20 heads, with DDI 0.627 and Dice 0.186. Both anatomical targets reached the operational 0.20 V/m floor in 11/20 versus 20/20 heads, respectively. ROAST 4.0, with ring placement held fixed, supported both nominations but exposed dose disagreement. Across conductivity sensitivity draws, directional separability persisted more consistently than absolute dose. These results establish a regional separability-dose trade-off within the tested candidate set and show why a summed contrast cannot substitute for a directional conjunction. They support selection of a discriminating experiment, not whole-network selectivity, physiological efficacy, or a validated treatment.
pending_articles.author: Bruschi, D. L., Schiavi, A., Joseph, I.

pending_articles.title: Braintree: An agentic framework for in-silico vision neuroscience
pending_articles.content: Vision neuroscience has many of the ingredients needed to conduct experiments entirely in-silico. We need AI systems that can reason over scientific knowledge, generative methods for creating precisely controlled stimuli, image-computable models that can predict neural responses with increasing accuracy, and tools that can analyze and interpret data. Here we take the first step toward making a vision neuroscience experiment end-to-end computable. We introduce Braintree, an agentic framework that can autonomously run multi-experiment studies directly with in-silico models of human visual cortex. Given a hypothesis, Braintree can reason over the current literature, design an experiment, build a stimulus set from algorithmically manipulated or synthesized stimuli, run the experiment on candidate brain encoding models, analyze the responses and then use the results to design even stronger tests. The entire loop runs autonomously and can accept human input at any stage. We evaluated Braintree on three increasingly open-ended scientific problems. First, Braintree reproduced published findings using their original stimuli and then asked whether the same effects could be replicated with entirely new stimulus sets that it constructed. Second, it designed new experiments to find stimulus dimensions that could drive two brain regions differently, even when those regions otherwise had similar response profiles. Third, it searched for experiments that could tell competing models of the same brain region apart. Experiments discovered using just two models also exposed differences across a much broader set of models, suggesting that Braintree had found more general dimensions along which brain models disagree. Braintree can augment the capabilities of a vision neuroscientist as a verifier for existing hypotheses, a test-bed for new ideas, and/or a tool for generating stimuli that can discriminate between competing hypotheses or models of the brain. Braintree shows how AI agents and brain models can work together to make in-silico vision neuroscience experiment computable, allowing vision scientists to explore many more experiment conditions and identify the most informative ones to test on the human brain.
pending_articles.author: Deb, M., Wang, R., Dipani, A., Ratan Murty, N. A.

pending_articles.title: Decoupling of spontaneous and evoked activity in locus coeruleus neurons: early synaptic and ion-channel remodeling in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease
pending_articles.content: The locus coeruleus (LC) is among the earliest brain regions affected in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the mechanisms underlying its early vulnerability remain poorly understood. Clarifying synaptic and intrinsic dysfunction in LC noradrenergic (NE) neurons is essential to determine how noradrenergic circuit failure contributes to prodromal AD. We combined whole-cell patch-clamp recordings with quantitative immunofluorescence to examine synaptic transmission, firing properties, voltage-gated currents, and synaptic organization in LC/NE neurons from young 3xTg mice prior to substantial neurodegeneration. Young 3xTg mice exhibited reduced excitatory and enhanced inhibitory synaptic input onto LC/NE neurons. Consistent with these functional shifts, structural analysis revealed decreased densities of VGLUT2, PSD95, and paired VGLUT2-PSD95 puncta, alongside increased VGAT, gephyrin, and paired VGAT-gephyrin puncta. Despite this net synaptic suppression, LC/NE neurons displayed elevated spontaneous firing rates but a markedly reduced capacity to generate spike output during sustained depolarization. Voltage-clamp recordings revealed a diminished total voltage-gated K current density alongside reduced voltage-gated Na current density, without significant shifts in their voltage-dependence or kinetics. These biophysical alterations provide a mechanistic basis for the divergent firing phenotype: reduced K current; conductance likely facilitates spontaneous pacemaker activity, whereas diminished Na current; current constrains repetitive, input-driven spike generation. Together, these findings demonstrate that LC/NE neurons undergo coordinated synaptic and ion-channel remodeling during prodromal AD. This unique decoupling of spontaneous baseline activity from stimulus-evoked excitability may impair dynamic noradrenergic modulation, positioning early LC cellular dysfunction as a candidate driver of network instability and a novel therapeutic target.

recently_processed.title: New Paper: Using Multivariate Pattern Analysis to Increase Effect Sizes for ERP Amplitude Comparisons
recently_processed.content:
Carrasco, C. D., Bahle, B., Simmons, A. M., & Luck, S. J. (2024). Using multivariate pattern analysis to increase effect sizes for event-related potential analyses. Psychophysiology, 61, e14570. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.14570 [preprint]

Multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) can be used to “decode” subtle information from ERP signals, such as which of several faces a participant is perceiving or the orientation that someone is holding in working memory (see this previous blog post). This approach is so powerful that we started wondering whether it might also give us greater statistical power in more typical experiments where the goal is to determine whether an ERP component differs in amplitude across experimental conditions. For example, might we more easily be able to tell if N400 amplitude is different between two different classes of words by using decoding? If so, that might make it possible to detect effects that would otherwise be too small to be significant.

To address this question, we compared decoding with the conventional ERP analysis approach with using the 6 experimental paradigms in the ERP CORE. In the conventional ERP analysis, we measured the mean amplitude during the standard measurement window from each participant in the two conditions of the paradigm (e.g., faces versus cars for N170, deviants versus standards for MMN). We quantified the magnitude of the difference between conditions using Cohen’s dz (the variant of Cohen’s d corresponding to a paired t test). For example, the effect size in the conventional ERP comparison of faces versus cars in the N170 paradigm was approximately 1.7 (see the figure).

We also applied decoding to each paradigm. For example, in the N170 paradigm, we trained a support vector machine (SVM) to distinguish between ERPs elicited by faces and ERPs elicited by cars. This was done separately for each subject, and we converted the decoding accuracy into Cohen’s dz so that it could be compared with the dz from the conventional ERP analysis. As you can see from the bar labeled SVM in the figure above, the effect size for the SVM-based decoding analysis was almost twice as large as the effect size for the conventional ERP analysis. That’s a huge difference!

We found a similar benefit for SVM-based decoding over conventional ERP analyses in 7 of the 10 cases we tested (see the figure below). In the other 3 cases, the ERP and SVM effects were approximately equivalent. So, there doesn’t seem to be a downside to using decoding, at least in terms of effect size. But there can be a big benefit.

Because decoding has many possible benefits, we’ve added it into ERPLAB Toolbox. It’s super easy to use, and we’ve created detailed documentation and a video to explain how it works at a conceptual level and to show you how to use it.

We encourage you to apply it to your own data. It may give you the power to detect effects that are too small to be detected with conventional ERP analyses.

recently_processed.title: An Information Compass for Probabilistic Reasoning in the Brain
recently_processed.content: Probabilistic reasoning in the brain has been studied primarily using simple two-choice tasks that are experimentally and theoretically tractable but have unclear relevance to more complex problems. Here we generalize principles from these studies using information geometry, which treats probability distributions (``beliefs'') as points on statistical manifolds whose geometry captures relationships between those beliefs. We introduce an ``information compass,'' a context-dependent, one-dimensional axis along which an arbitrarily complex belief is reinforced or repudiated. Projecting high-dimensional belief updates onto this axis casts even complex decisions into familiar forms of deliberation and commitment used for simpler decisions. Our framework provides a unified account of how biological and artificial systems can use geometric forms of probabilistic reasoning to make decisions across a range of tasks and domains.
recently_processed.author: Bosulu, J., Balasubramanian, V., Kilpatrick, Z. P., Josic, K., Gold, J. I.

recently_processed.title: Task-State Governance: A Virtual Machine for Verifiable and Recoverable GUI Agent Execution
recently_processed.content:
arXiv:2610.20100v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents now execute workflows across real applications, but when execution drifts, users must determine what changed, what should have remained untouched, and what can still be recovered. Plan-centric interfaces leave users supervising procedure, but users live with changes to application state. We introduce task-state governance, an interaction paradigm that represents a task as an editable contract linking desired outcomes, facts that must be preserved, and observed application state. We instantiate this paradigm in TaskVM, which projects live state into editable task controls, executes user edits as genuine interface actions, verifies outcomes through independent observation, and marks each action as reversible, compensatable, or irreversible. Across an automated contract benchmark, a controlled user study, and an open live-model exploration, the paradigm strengthened contract compliance and users' recovery control and trust, while execution outcomes were held constant. Task contracts open a design space for governable agent interfaces.
recently_processed.author: Wenkui Yang, Yiming Hao, Kai Zhou, Chengyu Pu, Yuzhe Zhang, Jie Cao, Jin Huang, Shuai Ma, Feng Tian

recently_processed.title: Scoping the Landscape of Large Language Model-based Affective Personal Informatics: Review, Reflection, Future Direction
recently_processed.content:
arXiv:2610.20084v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Affective personal informatics (PI) involves capturing, tracking, analyzing, and reflecting on personal data to support emotional self-awareness and mental well-being. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) are reshaping affective PI, yet a comprehensive survey of LLM-based affective PI systems is lacking. To bridge this gap, we systematically analyzed 45 papers published between January 2020 and June 2026 across four major computing and health databases, examining their macro trends, system taxonomies, and research methodologies. Our synthesis reveals an overreliance on multi-stage, text-centric pipelines, a predominance of active, screen-bound interactions, and a severe demographic skew toward young, university-campus-based cohorts in empirical evaluations. Based on these findings, we critically reflect on prevailing architectural and methodological shortcomings and outline actionable future directions for building end-to-end multimodal, low-burden, and inclusive affective PI systems.
recently_processed.author: Minjie Liu, Lihuan Li, Xuran Li, Flora Salim, Benjamin Tag

recently_processed.title: ShadAR: Real-time Prompting On-demand Visual Augmentation in Augmented Reality
recently_processed.content:
arXiv:2610.19998v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Augmented Reality can reshape our visual perception (e.g., simulating color blindness) yet such effects are typically pre-programmed by experts, making visual augmentation static and inflexible. We introduce ShadAR, an AR system that allows users to describe expected visual augmentations (e.g., "Blur all people") for changing their vision in real time. ShadAR can graphically manipulate AR passthrough in real time via shader injection. When receiving a user's prompt, ShadAR uses LLMs (GPT5.2) to interpret the user's intent, analyzes the user's view with object detection (YOLOv26), generates a pixel shader, and applies it to the targeted region on AR passthrough. To understand usage patterns, we invited 21 HCI researchers to use ShadAR, identifying four application domains (design, health, productivity, and social interaction) and two prompt-framing patterns: procedural prompts specifying what to modify and how ("Highlight the book."), and end-goal prompts conveying desired mental or behavioral states ("Make me laugh."). Such end-goal prompts suggest a future in which users specify outcomes (e.g., "Make me not miss my flight") while the system determines how to realize them, though often with inherently indeterminate results. We discuss design opportunities for ShadAR and ethical concerns.
recently_processed.author: Yanni Mei, Samuel Hartenstein, Jonas Wombacher, Florian Mueller, Jan Gugenheimer

recently_processed.title: Think Once, Reflect Twice: How Feedback Shapes Human-AI Collaboration
recently_processed.content:
arXiv:2610.19991v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly supports human decision-making in high-stakes domains, designing effective human-AI collaboration becomes critical. Successful collaboration requires humans to reflect on decision-making processes and adjust their strategies accordingly. Current research typically investigates interventions, such as explainable AI, that target reflection during the decision-making process (reflection-in-action). Less attention has been given to retrospective examination of decisions (reflection-on-action). This work explores reflection-on-action by studying the impact of feedback on reliance behavior and human-AI team performance. Specifically, we investigate feedback interventions targeting overrides of AI advice through a behavioral study (N=244). We find that such feedback influences reflection-on-action, while unidirectional feedback risks reducing subsequent reflection-in-action. Furthermore, we identify opposing shifts in reliance behavior that leave overall human-AI team performance unchanged but show context-dependent effects. Balanced feedback did not show these risks, preserving both concurrent and retrospective reflection, offering insights for designing for appropriate reliance on AI.
recently_processed.author: Joshua Holstein, Philipp Spitzer, Sebastian Sch\"afer, Maximilian F\"orster, Gerhard Satzger

recently_processed.title: AdaptaFace: Adversarial Assistance for Inclusive Facial Gesture Interaction
recently_processed.content:
arXiv:2610.19977v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Facial gestures can enable access for people with motor impairments (PwM), yet recognizers may not reliably interpret individual facial movement patterns. Existing approaches either constrain agency by requiring predefined templates or impose repeated calibration, data collection, and computation through user-specific retraining. We present AdaptaFace, an input-level compatibility layer using bounded, proxy-dependent adversarial perturbations to translate user-compatible gestures into inputs for an unchanged facial action unit (AU)-based recognizer. Designed around six personalization principles informed by interviews with 12 PwM, AdaptaFace supports both recognition enhancement and gesture vocabulary extension. In a within-subject study with 16 participants, AdaptaFace increased task completion from 59.7% to 90.5% and reduced workload from 5.61 to 4.21. Offline validation showed strong steering with aligned perturbation generation and evaluation but weaker cross-recognizer transfer, defining the approach's boundary. These findings frame adversarial assistance as input-side accessibility mediation for personalized facial-gesture interaction.
recently_processed.author: Siyu Zhang, Yelu Gu, Xiaoyun Xu, Kirsten Cater, Oussama Metatla
